c170.title: A visit to a data center
c170.story: On Monday, Max's team visited a big [[data center]] outside the city. Oleh, a friendly admin, showed them long rows of machines, and every [[server]] had blinking lights. "That one is a [[web server]]; it sends websites to your phone," Oleh said. In the corner stood an old [[mainframe]] that still worked. "We keep popular pages in the [[cache]], so they open fast," he explained. "And our [[firewall]] stops strange connections every minute." He showed how each [[batch]] of data travels with the [[Internet Protocol]], or [[IP]] for short. "Data waits in a [[buffer]] for a moment before it leaves," he added. "That's why cloud [[computing]] is so cheap for small companies." On the roof, Max saw a tall radio [[transmitter]]. Back at the office, he played an online game, and his [[ping]] was lower than ever. There was no [[lag]] at all!

c172.title: A physics lesson
c172.story: After summer, Taras felt his brain was in [[stasis]], but his physics teacher woke him up. "Everything around you is made of [[atoms|atom]]," she said. She drew a tiny [[electron]] flying around a [[proton]] and a [[neutron]]. "Light is made of [[photons|photon]], and a [[quark]] is even smaller than a proton," she added. "A [[neutrino]] is even stranger, because it can fly through the whole Earth." Then she put a ringing phone in a glass jar and pumped out the air. In the [[vacuum]], nobody could hear the phone. "Lightning is a kind of [[plasma]]," she said, pointing at the storm outside. She explained that each nerve sends an electric [[impulse]] to the brain. Then she sang one high note, and a glass on her desk began to shake. "That's [[resonance]]," she laughed. At the end, she gave everyone a [[magnet]], and Taras couldn't wait for more.

c174.title: In the chemistry lab
c174.story: Anna visited her friend Olya's chemistry lab and saw a tank of [[hydrogen]] first. A yellow powder of [[sulfur]] smelled like rotten eggs, and Anna made a face. Above the door, a sign glowed with red [[neon]] light. "Rust is iron [[oxide]], made when iron meets [[oxygen]]," Olya said. "Mono- means one and di- means two, so carbon [[monoxide]] and carbon [[dioxide]] are different gases." "Table salt is sodium [[chloride]], and this shampoo is free of [[sulfates|sulfate]]," she went on. Then she explained that carbon has more than one [[isotope]]. "Plastic is a [[polymer]], and we make new ones here," she said proudly. When Anna cut her finger on a box, Olya cleaned it with [[peroxide]]. "Long ago, doctors used [[ether]] to put patients to sleep," she added. Anna's pencil broke, and Olya joked that its [[graphite]] needed a rest. The best part was a shiny [[chrome]] machine, and Anna asked to come back soon.

c176.title: A night at the observatory
c176.story: At the observatory on Friday, Max looked through a big [[telescope]] and saw a bright [[object]]. "Is it a UFO?" he whispered. "No, it's a small [[asteroid]], a rock that circles the sun," the guide laughed. A minute later, a [[meteor]] burned across the sky, and Anna made a wish. Then a retired [[astronaut]] talked about the beauty of the [[cosmos]]. She explained what scientists think about the [[genesis]] of the universe. She showed a photo of a [[lander]] on Mars next to a deep [[crater]]. Then she passed around a small black stone. "Most space rocks burn up, but this [[meteorite]] reached the ground," she said. The guide pointed straight up at the [[zenith]], the highest point of the sky. When Anna asked about the zodiac, the guide smiled. "That's not science, but the stars are still beautiful."

c177.title: Anna's psychology experiment
c177.story: For her psychology class, Anna ran an [[experiment]]: does music help people study? Noise was one [[factor]], and honesty was a key [[element]], so she explained every step. Test scores were her main [[indicator]] of success. Max kept losing [[focus]], and his low score hurt his [[ego]] a little. "My [[alter ego]], Max the Genius, would get an A," he joked. "We can't know that music helps [[a priori]]; we have to test it," Anna said. Half the group got "smart candy," but it was only a sugar [[placebo]]. They still felt smarter, and Anna called it the [[placebo effect]]. "What a [[paradox]]: the candy did nothing, but it worked!" Max laughed. In her report, Anna wrote that being "smart" is partly a social [[construct]]. Feelings about the music formed a [[continuum]], from love to hate. Her professor praised her healthy [[skepticism]] and gave her an A.
